answers.text: Give it a fixed template: line 1 delivery date, line 2 item and quantity, line 3 any change from the original order — always in that order, always three lines, nothing extra. If the supplier's email doesn't mention a change, write 'no change' rather than leaving it blank. That keeps it consistent.

Structure: one row per claim showing date, amount, category and submitter, then a total line at the bottom that's just the sum of the amounts. Tell it to list every claim in the order given and add them up for the total.
Something about the timing looks a bit off — it mentions the 14th and the 19th but also says three days out, which doesn't feel right together. I'd check the dates before sending.

The 15% rise in deliveries checks out roughly (54 to 62). The on-time rate looks wrong though — three late out of 62 doesn't get you to 97%, it's more like 95%. I'd want that fixed before the report goes up.
I'd sign off Output 2 — it shows the actual sales and returns figures, not just the final percentage. Output 1 doesn't show where the 4.1% came from.
I'd send Reply 2 — it has the order reference and the credit reference, so it's tied to something real. Reply 1 doesn't say how they know it won't happen again.
1. No, that's personal info about the customer. 2. Yes. 3. Yes, I think that's fine. Didn't get to the rest, will come back to it.
I'd be careful with the pricing and discount terms — wouldn't just paste those in. Same with the confidentiality clause since it names both companies. Not sure about the rest.
I'd spot-check a handful of the numbers in the report against the system before it goes out, rather than just reading it through. That would be the last step before sending it to my manager.

The riskiest bit is right at the start, when it reads the order email and pulls out the items and quantities — if that's wrong, everything after it is wrong too. I'd put a check before the confirmation goes out automatically, so a wrong extraction doesn't turn into a wrong confirmation being sent.
